## Question 331 — Bundle regression

**Module:** Module 19 – Production Scenarios  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐ Medium  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Bundle regression** to a senior frontend interviewer, and how would you apply it safely in a production React 19+ TypeScript application?

### Definition
Bundle regression should be understood at API, rendering, runtime and production-architecture levels. A senior engineer should be able to explain its trade-offs, measure its impact, debug failures and choose whether the abstraction belongs in the system.

### Overview
Explain the public React API first, then the rendering consequence, then the production trade-offs. Avoid presenting unstable implementation details as guaranteed public behavior.

### Why It Matters
- It affects correctness, responsiveness, maintainability or scalability.
- Senior interviews expect trade-off analysis, not API memorization.
- Enterprise systems require observability, testing, accessibility and safe migration paths.

### React Internal Behavior
Where applicable, React schedules work, builds/reconciles Fiber trees during rendering, then applies host mutations and runs relevant commit-time work. The exact internal implementation is version-dependent.

### Fiber / Scheduler Flow
```text
Update
  ↓
Priority / Scheduling
  ↓
Work-in-progress Fiber
  ↓
Reconciliation
  ↓
Render
  ↓
Commit
  ↓
Host Environment
```

### Code Example 1
```tsx
type Props = { title: string };

export function Feature({ title }: Props) {
  return <section aria-labelledby="feature-title">
    <h2 id="feature-title">{title}</h2>
  </section>;
}
```

### Code Example 2 — Production Pattern
tsx
import { memo } from "react";

type UserRowProps = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  onOpen: (id: string) => void;
};

export const UserRow = memo(function UserRow({
  id,
  name,
  onOpen,
}: UserRowProps) {
  return (
    <li>
      <span>{name}</span>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => onOpen(id)}>
        Open
      </button>
    </li>
  );
});
```

### Production Example
For a large enterprise application, isolate this concern behind a small feature API, instrument important failures, test user-visible behavior, and measure render/network/browser costs before optimizing.

### Expected Output
The component produces the expected accessible UI. When inputs change, React may schedule rendering work and reconcile the resulting tree before committing necessary host updates.

### Execution Flow
```text
Props / State / Context
          ↓
       Component
          ↓
      React Elements
          ↓
   Fiber Reconciliation
          ↓
      Render Phase
          ↓
      Commit Phase
          ↓
       Host DOM
          ↓
    Browser Rendering
```

### Component Tree
```text
<App>
 ├── <Shell>
 │    ├── <Navigation>
 │    └── <Content>
 └── <Footer>
```

### Fiber Diagram
```text
Fiber Root
   │
   ├── Fiber(App)
   │      ├── Fiber(Header)
   │      └── Fiber(Main)
   │             └── Fiber(Feature)
   │
   └── alternate → work-in-progress tree
```

### Scheduler Timeline
```text
Urgent input ───────► render/commit
                         │
Non-urgent work ───► can be scheduled around higher-priority work
```

### Advantages
- Clear declarative model
- Strong composition
- Supports scalable UI architecture
- Rich profiling and testing ecosystem

### Disadvantages / Trade-offs
- Abstractions can be overused.
- Rendering behavior can become difficult to reason about in very large trees.
- Performance optimizations add complexity and should be justified by measurement.

### Performance Considerations
- Profile before adding memoization.
- Separate network, CPU, render, commit and browser paint costs.
- Use code splitting and virtualization for the appropriate bottleneck.
- Watch memory retention from subscriptions, closures, caches and long-lived providers.

### Accessibility Considerations
- Prefer native HTML semantics.
- Preserve keyboard and screen-reader behavior.
- Provide accessible loading, error and status states.
- Ensure focus is managed when UI boundaries change.

### Security Considerations
- Treat server data and user input as untrusted.
- Avoid unsafe HTML injection.
- Do not expose secrets in Client Components or browser bundles.
- Audit server/client boundaries and authorization independently of UI visibility.

### Best Practices
- Keep components focused and composable.
- Keep render logic pure.
- Keep state close to its owner.
- Use stable keys for dynamic collections.
- Prefer explicit data boundaries.
- Add telemetry at important production failure boundaries.

### Anti-patterns
- Global state for every value
- Effects used for derived values
- Blind `useMemo` / `useCallback`
- Giant context providers
- Index keys for reorderable lists
- Client-side secrets

### Common Mistakes
- Treating Fiber fields as stable public APIs.
- Assuming a render always equals a DOM mutation.
- Ignoring cleanup and cancellation.
- Optimizing without profiling.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce with the smallest possible component tree.  
2. Use React DevTools Components and Profiler panels.  
3. Inspect props/state/context changes.  
4. Record a performance profile.  
5. Check browser Performance and Network panels.  
6. Add targeted logs rather than broad console noise.

### Common Interview Traps
- Confusing render phase and commit phase.
- Saying concurrent rendering means concurrent DOM mutations.
- Treating `useMemo` as a semantic guarantee.
- Assuming Context is automatically a global-state replacement.

### Scenario-Based Question
A production application has a regression involving **Bundle regression**. Explain how you would identify the root cause, profile it, validate a fix and prevent recurrence.

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the alternative and why did you reject it?
2. What happens during render versus commit?
3. What is the memory cost?
4. How would React DevTools expose the problem?
5. How would you test the behavior?
6. What would change at 10× application scale?
7. What metrics would you monitor in production?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion
Define ownership, API boundaries, observability, testing, rollout strategy and failure recovery. For shared infrastructure, document the contract and migration plan before making the abstraction universal.

### System Design Discussion
Design the feature as independently deployable or testable where appropriate. Keep server data, client UI state and cross-cutting configuration distinct. Establish clear performance budgets and failure boundaries.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] Correct React API usage
- [ ] Render logic is pure
- [ ] Cleanup exists for subscriptions/resources
- [ ] Accessibility reviewed
- [ ] Error/loading states handled
- [ ] No unnecessary global state
- [ ] Performance measured where optimization is claimed
- [ ] Tests cover user-visible behavior

### Comparison Table
| Area | Preferred | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| State | Local ownership first | Global by default |
| Performance | Measure → optimize | Blind memoization |
| Async | Cancellation/recovery | Unbounded requests |
| Components | Composition | Deep inheritance |
| Lists | Stable identity keys | Index for mutable lists |

### 30-Second Interview Answer
**Bundle regression** should be explained from its React API, rendering behavior and production trade-offs. I would show a small TypeScript example, explain what React schedules and commits, then cover performance, accessibility, testing and failure handling.

### 2-Minute Interview Answer
Start with the definition of **Bundle regression**, show the simplest correct implementation, then trace the update through React's render/reconciliation and commit model. Finish with profiling, testing, accessibility, security and the enterprise architecture trade-offs.

### 5-Minute Deep Explanation
At Staff/Principal level, explain **Bundle regression** as a system design concern: API contract, component boundaries, scheduling/reconciliation implications, browser interaction, memory behavior, failure modes, observability, testing, performance budget, rollout strategy and migration cost. Explicitly separate stable public React behavior from implementation details.

### Assignment
Build a production-grade TypeScript React 19 feature demonstrating **Bundle regression**. Add tests, accessible states, error handling, profiling notes and a short architecture decision record.

### Production Exercise
Create a before/after performance profile or architecture comparison. Record the measured bottleneck, selected optimization, regression risk and verification method.

### Mini Project
Build a small enterprise feature around **Bundle regression** with feature-based folders, typed APIs, reusable components, tests and observability hooks.

### MCQs
1. Which React phase determines the work needed for the next UI tree?  
A. Render  B. Browser paint  C. DNS  D. CSS parsing  
**Answer: A**
2. Which is the best reason to use memoization?  
A. It is always required  B. Measured reduction in expensive work  C. It changes semantics  D. It prevents all renders  
**Answer: B**
3. What should a dynamic list key represent?  
A. Array index  B. Random number  C. Stable item identity  D. CSS class  
**Answer: C**
4. What is a key concurrency goal?  
A. Make every update synchronous  B. Keep urgent interactions responsive while scheduling non-urgent work  C. Remove the DOM  D. Disable effects  
**Answer: B**
5. What is a production security boundary?  
A. UI hiding  B. Server authorization  C. CSS  D. Memoization  
**Answer: B**

### Coding Exercise
Implement **Bundle regression** in TypeScript with an accessible UI, error handling, stable state ownership and a test. Explain render behavior and one performance trade-off.

### Debugging Exercise
Capture a React DevTools Profiler trace, identify the component with the highest relevant render/commit cost, change one variable at a time, and compare before/after measurements.

### Revision Notes
- Bundle regression: know API → render behavior → commit behavior → performance → accessibility → testing → enterprise trade-offs.
- Distinguish stable React contracts from implementation details.

### Cheat Sheet
**Bundle regression → API → identity → scheduling → render → commit → browser → memory → performance → testing → architecture**

## Question 334 — Incident response

**Module:** Module 19 – Production Scenarios  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Staff / Principal  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Incident response** to a senior frontend interviewer, and how would you apply it safely in a production React 19+ TypeScript application?

### Definition
Incident response should be understood at API, rendering, runtime and production-architecture levels. A senior engineer should be able to explain its trade-offs, measure its impact, debug failures and choose whether the abstraction belongs in the system.

### Overview
Explain the public React API first, then the rendering consequence, then the production trade-offs. Avoid presenting unstable implementation details as guaranteed public behavior.

### Why It Matters
- It affects correctness, responsiveness, maintainability or scalability.
- Senior interviews expect trade-off analysis, not API memorization.
- Enterprise systems require observability, testing, accessibility and safe migration paths.

### React Internal Behavior
Where applicable, React schedules work, builds/reconciles Fiber trees during rendering, then applies host mutations and runs relevant commit-time work. The exact internal implementation is version-dependent.

### Fiber / Scheduler Flow
```text
Update
  ↓
Priority / Scheduling
  ↓
Work-in-progress Fiber
  ↓
Reconciliation
  ↓
Render
  ↓
Commit
  ↓
Host Environment
```

### Code Example 1
```tsx
type Props = { title: string };

export function Feature({ title }: Props) {
  return <section aria-labelledby="feature-title">
    <h2 id="feature-title">{title}</h2>
  </section>;
}
```

### Code Example 2 — Production Pattern
tsx
import { memo } from "react";

type UserRowProps = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  onOpen: (id: string) => void;
};

export const UserRow = memo(function UserRow({
  id,
  name,
  onOpen,
}: UserRowProps) {
  return (
    <li>
      <span>{name}</span>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => onOpen(id)}>
        Open
      </button>
    </li>
  );
});
```

### Production Example
For a large enterprise application, isolate this concern behind a small feature API, instrument important failures, test user-visible behavior, and measure render/network/browser costs before optimizing.

### Expected Output
The component produces the expected accessible UI. When inputs change, React may schedule rendering work and reconcile the resulting tree before committing necessary host updates.

### Execution Flow
```text
Props / State / Context
          ↓
       Component
          ↓
      React Elements
          ↓
   Fiber Reconciliation
          ↓
      Render Phase
          ↓
      Commit Phase
          ↓
       Host DOM
          ↓
    Browser Rendering
```

### Component Tree
```text
<App>
 ├── <Shell>
 │    ├── <Navigation>
 │    └── <Content>
 └── <Footer>
```

### Fiber Diagram
```text
Fiber Root
   │
   ├── Fiber(App)
   │      ├── Fiber(Header)
   │      └── Fiber(Main)
   │             └── Fiber(Feature)
   │
   └── alternate → work-in-progress tree
```

### Scheduler Timeline
```text
Urgent input ───────► render/commit
                         │
Non-urgent work ───► can be scheduled around higher-priority work
```

### Advantages
- Clear declarative model
- Strong composition
- Supports scalable UI architecture
- Rich profiling and testing ecosystem

### Disadvantages / Trade-offs
- Abstractions can be overused.
- Rendering behavior can become difficult to reason about in very large trees.
- Performance optimizations add complexity and should be justified by measurement.

### Performance Considerations
- Profile before adding memoization.
- Separate network, CPU, render, commit and browser paint costs.
- Use code splitting and virtualization for the appropriate bottleneck.
- Watch memory retention from subscriptions, closures, caches and long-lived providers.

### Accessibility Considerations
- Prefer native HTML semantics.
- Preserve keyboard and screen-reader behavior.
- Provide accessible loading, error and status states.
- Ensure focus is managed when UI boundaries change.

### Security Considerations
- Treat server data and user input as untrusted.
- Avoid unsafe HTML injection.
- Do not expose secrets in Client Components or browser bundles.
- Audit server/client boundaries and authorization independently of UI visibility.

### Best Practices
- Keep components focused and composable.
- Keep render logic pure.
- Keep state close to its owner.
- Use stable keys for dynamic collections.
- Prefer explicit data boundaries.
- Add telemetry at important production failure boundaries.

### Anti-patterns
- Global state for every value
- Effects used for derived values
- Blind `useMemo` / `useCallback`
- Giant context providers
- Index keys for reorderable lists
- Client-side secrets

### Common Mistakes
- Treating Fiber fields as stable public APIs.
- Assuming a render always equals a DOM mutation.
- Ignoring cleanup and cancellation.
- Optimizing without profiling.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce with the smallest possible component tree.  
2. Use React DevTools Components and Profiler panels.  
3. Inspect props/state/context changes.  
4. Record a performance profile.  
5. Check browser Performance and Network panels.  
6. Add targeted logs rather than broad console noise.

### Common Interview Traps
- Confusing render phase and commit phase.
- Saying concurrent rendering means concurrent DOM mutations.
- Treating `useMemo` as a semantic guarantee.
- Assuming Context is automatically a global-state replacement.

### Scenario-Based Question
A production application has a regression involving **Incident response**. Explain how you would identify the root cause, profile it, validate a fix and prevent recurrence.

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the alternative and why did you reject it?
2. What happens during render versus commit?
3. What is the memory cost?
4. How would React DevTools expose the problem?
5. How would you test the behavior?
6. What would change at 10× application scale?
7. What metrics would you monitor in production?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion
Define ownership, API boundaries, observability, testing, rollout strategy and failure recovery. For shared infrastructure, document the contract and migration plan before making the abstraction universal.

### System Design Discussion
Design the feature as independently deployable or testable where appropriate. Keep server data, client UI state and cross-cutting configuration distinct. Establish clear performance budgets and failure boundaries.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] Correct React API usage
- [ ] Render logic is pure
- [ ] Cleanup exists for subscriptions/resources
- [ ] Accessibility reviewed
- [ ] Error/loading states handled
- [ ] No unnecessary global state
- [ ] Performance measured where optimization is claimed
- [ ] Tests cover user-visible behavior

### Comparison Table
| Area | Preferred | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| State | Local ownership first | Global by default |
| Performance | Measure → optimize | Blind memoization |
| Async | Cancellation/recovery | Unbounded requests |
| Components | Composition | Deep inheritance |
| Lists | Stable identity keys | Index for mutable lists |

**Answer: B**
3. What should a dynamic list key represent?

**Answer: C**
4. What is a key concurrency goal?  
A. Make every update synchronous  B. Keep urgent interactions responsive while scheduling non-urgent work  C. Remove the DOM  D. Disable effects  
**Answer: B**
5. What is a production security boundary?  
A. UI hiding  B. Server authorization  C. CSS  D. Memoization  
**Answer: B**

## Question 337 — Fiber revision

**Module:** Module 20 – Final Revision  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐ Hard  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Fiber revision** to a senior frontend interviewer, and how would you apply it safely in a production React 19+ TypeScript application?

### Definition
Fiber is React's internal unit of work and data structure for representing component work. It enables React to track work, prioritize it, reconcile trees and coordinate rendering with the scheduler.

### Overview
Explain the public React API first, then the rendering consequence, then the production trade-offs. Avoid presenting unstable implementation details as guaranteed public behavior.

### Why It Matters
- It affects correctness, responsiveness, maintainability or scalability.
- Senior interviews expect trade-off analysis, not API memorization.
- Enterprise systems require observability, testing, accessibility and safe migration paths.

### React Internal Behavior
Where applicable, React schedules work, builds/reconciles Fiber trees during rendering, then applies host mutations and runs relevant commit-time work. The exact internal implementation is version-dependent.

### Fiber / Scheduler Flow
```text
Update
  ↓
Priority / Scheduling
  ↓
Work-in-progress Fiber
  ↓
Reconciliation
  ↓
Render
  ↓
Commit
  ↓
Host Environment
```

### Code Example 1
```tsx
type Props = { title: string };

export function Feature({ title }: Props) {
  return <section aria-labelledby="feature-title">
    <h2 id="feature-title">{title}</h2>
  </section>;
}
```

### Code Example 2 — Production Pattern
tsx
import { memo } from "react";

type UserRowProps = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  onOpen: (id: string) => void;
};

export const UserRow = memo(function UserRow({
  id,
  name,
  onOpen,
}: UserRowProps) {
  return (
    <li>
      <span>{name}</span>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => onOpen(id)}>
        Open
      </button>
    </li>
  );
});
```

### Production Example
For a large enterprise application, isolate this concern behind a small feature API, instrument important failures, test user-visible behavior, and measure render/network/browser costs before optimizing.

### Expected Output
The component produces the expected accessible UI. When inputs change, React may schedule rendering work and reconcile the resulting tree before committing necessary host updates.

### Execution Flow
```text
Props / State / Context
          ↓
       Component
          ↓
      React Elements
          ↓
   Fiber Reconciliation
          ↓
      Render Phase
          ↓
      Commit Phase
          ↓
       Host DOM
          ↓
    Browser Rendering
```

### Component Tree
```text
<App>
 ├── <Shell>
 │    ├── <Navigation>
 │    └── <Content>
 └── <Footer>
```

### Fiber Diagram
```text
Fiber Root
   │
   ├── Fiber(App)
   │      ├── Fiber(Header)
   │      └── Fiber(Main)
   │             └── Fiber(Feature)
   │
   └── alternate → work-in-progress tree
```

### Scheduler Timeline
```text
Urgent input ───────► render/commit
                         │
Non-urgent work ───► can be scheduled around higher-priority work
```

### Advantages
- Clear declarative model
- Strong composition
- Supports scalable UI architecture
- Rich profiling and testing ecosystem

### Disadvantages / Trade-offs
- Abstractions can be overused.
- Rendering behavior can become difficult to reason about in very large trees.
- Performance optimizations add complexity and should be justified by measurement.

### Performance Considerations
- Profile before adding memoization.
- Separate network, CPU, render, commit and browser paint costs.
- Use code splitting and virtualization for the appropriate bottleneck.
- Watch memory retention from subscriptions, closures, caches and long-lived providers.

### Accessibility Considerations
- Prefer native HTML semantics.
- Preserve keyboard and screen-reader behavior.
- Provide accessible loading, error and status states.
- Ensure focus is managed when UI boundaries change.

### Security Considerations
- Treat server data and user input as untrusted.
- Avoid unsafe HTML injection.
- Do not expose secrets in Client Components or browser bundles.
- Audit server/client boundaries and authorization independently of UI visibility.

### Best Practices
- Keep components focused and composable.
- Keep render logic pure.
- Keep state close to its owner.
- Use stable keys for dynamic collections.
- Prefer explicit data boundaries.
- Add telemetry at important production failure boundaries.

### Anti-patterns
- Global state for every value
- Effects used for derived values
- Blind `useMemo` / `useCallback`
- Giant context providers
- Index keys for reorderable lists
- Client-side secrets

### Common Mistakes
- Treating Fiber fields as stable public APIs.
- Assuming a render always equals a DOM mutation.
- Ignoring cleanup and cancellation.
- Optimizing without profiling.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce with the smallest possible component tree.  
2. Use React DevTools Components and Profiler panels.  
3. Inspect props/state/context changes.  
4. Record a performance profile.  
5. Check browser Performance and Network panels.  
6. Add targeted logs rather than broad console noise.

### Common Interview Traps
- Confusing render phase and commit phase.
- Saying concurrent rendering means concurrent DOM mutations.
- Treating `useMemo` as a semantic guarantee.
- Assuming Context is automatically a global-state replacement.

### Scenario-Based Question
A production application has a regression involving **Fiber revision**. Explain how you would identify the root cause, profile it, validate a fix and prevent recurrence.

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the alternative and why did you reject it?
2. What happens during render versus commit?
3. What is the memory cost?
4. How would React DevTools expose the problem?
5. How would you test the behavior?
6. What would change at 10× application scale?
7. What metrics would you monitor in production?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion
Define ownership, API boundaries, observability, testing, rollout strategy and failure recovery. For shared infrastructure, document the contract and migration plan before making the abstraction universal.

### System Design Discussion
Design the feature as independently deployable or testable where appropriate. Keep server data, client UI state and cross-cutting configuration distinct. Establish clear performance budgets and failure boundaries.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] Correct React API usage
- [ ] Render logic is pure
- [ ] Cleanup exists for subscriptions/resources
- [ ] Accessibility reviewed
- [ ] Error/loading states handled
- [ ] No unnecessary global state
- [ ] Performance measured where optimization is claimed
- [ ] Tests cover user-visible behavior

### Comparison Table
| Area | Preferred | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| State | Local ownership first | Global by default |
| Performance | Measure → optimize | Blind memoization |
| Async | Cancellation/recovery | Unbounded requests |
| Components | Composition | Deep inheritance |
| Lists | Stable identity keys | Index for mutable lists |

### Question
How would you explain **Context revision** to a senior frontend interviewer, and how would you apply it safely in a production React 19+ TypeScript application?

### Definition
Context propagates values through a component subtree. The key production concern is provider value identity: changing the value can invalidate consumers, so split contexts and stabilize values where measurement shows benefit.

### Overview

  ↓

```tsx
import { createContext, useContext, useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Session = { userId: string } | null;
const SessionContext = createContext<Session>(null);

export function SessionProvider({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const [session] = useState<Session>({ userId: "u-1" });
  const value = useMemo(() => session, [session]);

  return (
    <SessionContext.Provider value={value}>
      {children}
    </SessionContext.Provider>
  );
}

export function useSession() {
  return useContext(SessionContext);
}
```

## Question 340 — Error handling revision

**Module:** Module 20 – Final Revision  
**Difficulty:** ⭐ Easy  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Error handling revision** to a senior frontend interviewer, and how would you apply it safely in a production React 19+ TypeScript application?

### Definition
Error handling should classify failures by where they occur: render, event handlers, async operations, network boundaries and route boundaries. Use recovery UI and centralized telemetry without exposing sensitive data.

### Overview
Explain the public React API first, then the rendering consequence, then the production trade-offs. Avoid presenting unstable implementation details as guaranteed public behavior.

### Why It Matters
- It affects correctness, responsiveness, maintainability or scalability.
- Senior interviews expect trade-off analysis, not API memorization.
- Enterprise systems require observability, testing, accessibility and safe migration paths.

### React Internal Behavior
Where applicable, React schedules work, builds/reconciles Fiber trees during rendering, then applies host mutations and runs relevant commit-time work. The exact internal implementation is version-dependent.

### Fiber / Scheduler Flow
```text
Update
  ↓
Priority / Scheduling
  ↓
Work-in-progress Fiber
  ↓
Reconciliation
  ↓
Render
  ↓
Commit
  ↓
Host Environment
```

### Code Example 1
```tsx
import { Component, type ErrorInfo, type ReactNode } from "react";

export class ErrorBoundary extends Component<
  { children: ReactNode },
  { hasError: boolean }
> {
  state = { hasError: false };

  static getDerivedStateFromError() {
    return { hasError: true };
  }

  componentDidCatch(error: Error, info: ErrorInfo) {
    console.error("UI error", error, info);
  }

  render() {
    return this.state.hasError
      ? <p role="alert">Something went wrong.</p>
      : this.props.children;
  }
}
```

### Code Example 2 — Production Pattern
tsx
import { memo } from "react";

type UserRowProps = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  onOpen: (id: string) => void;
};

export const UserRow = memo(function UserRow({
  id,
  name,
  onOpen,
}: UserRowProps) {
  return (
    <li>
      <span>{name}</span>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => onOpen(id)}>
        Open
      </button>
    </li>
  );
});
```

### Production Example
For a large enterprise application, isolate this concern behind a small feature API, instrument important failures, test user-visible behavior, and measure render/network/browser costs before optimizing.

### Expected Output
The component produces the expected accessible UI. When inputs change, React may schedule rendering work and reconcile the resulting tree before committing necessary host updates.

### Execution Flow
```text
Props / State / Context
          ↓
       Component
          ↓
      React Elements
          ↓
   Fiber Reconciliation
          ↓
      Render Phase
          ↓
      Commit Phase
          ↓
       Host DOM
          ↓
    Browser Rendering
```

### Component Tree
```text
<App>
 ├── <Shell>
 │    ├── <Navigation>
 │    └── <Content>
 └── <Footer>
```

### Fiber Diagram
```text
Fiber Root
   │
   ├── Fiber(App)
   │      ├── Fiber(Header)
   │      └── Fiber(Main)
   │             └── Fiber(Feature)
   │
   └── alternate → work-in-progress tree
```

### Scheduler Timeline
```text
Urgent input ───────► render/commit
                         │
Non-urgent work ───► can be scheduled around higher-priority work
```

### Advantages
- Clear declarative model
- Strong composition
- Supports scalable UI architecture
- Rich profiling and testing ecosystem

### Disadvantages / Trade-offs
- Abstractions can be overused.
- Rendering behavior can become difficult to reason about in very large trees.
- Performance optimizations add complexity and should be justified by measurement.

### Performance Considerations
- Profile before adding memoization.
- Separate network, CPU, render, commit and browser paint costs.
- Use code splitting and virtualization for the appropriate bottleneck.
- Watch memory retention from subscriptions, closures, caches and long-lived providers.

### Accessibility Considerations
- Prefer native HTML semantics.
- Preserve keyboard and screen-reader behavior.
- Provide accessible loading, error and status states.
- Ensure focus is managed when UI boundaries change.

### Security Considerations
- Treat server data and user input as untrusted.
- Avoid unsafe HTML injection.
- Do not expose secrets in Client Components or browser bundles.
- Audit server/client boundaries and authorization independently of UI visibility.

### Best Practices
- Keep components focused and composable.
- Keep render logic pure.
- Keep state close to its owner.
- Use stable keys for dynamic collections.
- Prefer explicit data boundaries.
- Add telemetry at important production failure boundaries.

### Anti-patterns
- Global state for every value
- Effects used for derived values
- Blind `useMemo` / `useCallback`
- Giant context providers
- Index keys for reorderable lists
- Client-side secrets

### Common Mistakes
- Treating Fiber fields as stable public APIs.
- Assuming a render always equals a DOM mutation.
- Ignoring cleanup and cancellation.
- Optimizing without profiling.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce with the smallest possible component tree.  
2. Use React DevTools Components and Profiler panels.  
3. Inspect props/state/context changes.  
4. Record a performance profile.  
5. Check browser Performance and Network panels.  
6. Add targeted logs rather than broad console noise.

### Common Interview Traps
- Confusing render phase and commit phase.
- Saying concurrent rendering means concurrent DOM mutations.
- Treating `useMemo` as a semantic guarantee.
- Assuming Context is automatically a global-state replacement.

3. What is the memory cost?
4. How would React DevTools expose the problem?
5. How would you test the behavior?

7. What metrics would you monitor in production?

## Question 342 — Concurrent React revision

**Module:** Module 20 – Final Revision  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐ Hard  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Concurrent React revision** to a senior frontend interviewer, and how would you apply it safely in a production React 19+ TypeScript application?

### Definition
Concurrent React is about scheduling rendering work so urgent updates can remain responsive while non-urgent rendering can be interrupted or deprioritized. It does not mean two DOM trees are simultaneously interactive.

### Overview
Explain the public React API first, then the rendering consequence, then the production trade-offs. Avoid presenting unstable implementation details as guaranteed public behavior.

  ↓
Work-in-progress Fiber
  ↓
Reconciliation
  ↓
Render
  ↓
Commit
  ↓
Host Environment
```

### Code Example 1
```tsx
import { useDeferredValue, useMemo, useState } from "react";

export function Search({ items }: { items: string[] }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);

  const filtered = useMemo(
    () => items.filter(item => item.toLowerCase().includes(deferredQuery.toLowerCase())),
    [items, deferredQuery],
  );

  return (
    <>
      <label>
        Search
        <input value={query} onChange={event => setQuery(event.target.value)} />
      </label>
      <p>{filtered.length} results</p>
    </>
  );
}
```

type UserRowProps = {

  name,
  onOpen,
}: UserRowProps) {
  return (
    <li>
      <span>{name}</span>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => onOpen(id)}>

});

2. Use React DevTools Components and Profiler panels.  
3. Inspect props/state/context changes.  
4. Record a performance profile.  
5. Check browser Performance and Network panels.  
6. Add targeted logs rather than broad console noise.

### Common Interview Traps
- Confusing render phase and commit phase.
- Saying concurrent rendering means concurrent DOM mutations.
- Treating `useMemo` as a semantic guarantee.
- Assuming Context is automatically a global-state replacement.

### Scenario-Based Question
A production application has a regression involving **Concurrent React revision**. Explain how you would identify the root cause, profile it, validate a fix and prevent recurrence.

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the alternative and why did you reject it?
2. What happens during render versus commit?
3. What is the memory cost?
4. How would React DevTools expose the problem?
5. How would you test the behavior?
6. What would change at 10× application scale?
7. What metrics would you monitor in production?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion
Define ownership, API boundaries, observability, testing, rollout strategy and failure recovery. For shared infrastructure, document the contract and migration plan before making the abstraction universal.

### System Design Discussion
Design the feature as independently deployable or testable where appropriate. Keep server data, client UI state and cross-cutting configuration distinct. Establish clear performance budgets and failure boundaries.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] Correct React API usage
- [ ] Render logic is pure
- [ ] Cleanup exists for subscriptions/resources
- [ ] Accessibility reviewed
- [ ] Error/loading states handled
- [ ] No unnecessary global state
- [ ] Performance measured where optimization is claimed
- [ ] Tests cover user-visible behavior

### Comparison Table

|---|---|---|
| State | Local ownership first | Global by default |
| Performance | Measure → optimize | Blind memoization |
| Async | Cancellation/recovery | Unbounded requests |
| Components | Composition | Deep inheritance |
| Lists | Stable identity keys | Index for mutable lists |

## Question 343 — React 19 revision

**Module:** Module 20 – Final Revision  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Senior  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **React 19 revision** to a senior frontend interviewer, and how would you apply it safely in a production React 19+ TypeScript application?

### Definition
React 19 revision should be understood at API, rendering, runtime and production-architecture levels. A senior engineer should be able to explain its trade-offs, measure its impact, debug failures and choose whether the abstraction belongs in the system.

### Overview
Explain the public React API first, then the rendering consequence, then the production trade-offs. Avoid presenting unstable implementation details as guaranteed public behavior.

### Why It Matters
- It affects correctness, responsiveness, maintainability or scalability.
- Senior interviews expect trade-off analysis, not API memorization.
- Enterprise systems require observability, testing, accessibility and safe migration paths.

### React Internal Behavior
Where applicable, React schedules work, builds/reconciles Fiber trees during rendering, then applies host mutations and runs relevant commit-time work. The exact internal implementation is version-dependent.

### Fiber / Scheduler Flow
```text
Update
  ↓
Priority / Scheduling
  ↓
Work-in-progress Fiber
  ↓
Reconciliation
  ↓
Render
  ↓
Commit
  ↓
Host Environment
```

### Code Example 1
```tsx
type Props = { title: string };

export function Feature({ title }: Props) {
  return <section aria-labelledby="feature-title">
    <h2 id="feature-title">{title}</h2>
  </section>;
}
```

### Code Example 2 — Production Pattern
tsx
import { memo } from "react";

type UserRowProps = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  onOpen: (id: string) => void;
};

export const UserRow = memo(function UserRow({
  id,
  name,
  onOpen,
}: UserRowProps) {
  return (
    <li>
      <span>{name}</span>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => onOpen(id)}>
        Open
      </button>
    </li>
  );
});
```

### Production Example
For a large enterprise application, isolate this concern behind a small feature API, instrument important failures, test user-visible behavior, and measure render/network/browser costs before optimizing.

### Expected Output
The component produces the expected accessible UI. When inputs change, React may schedule rendering work and reconcile the resulting tree before committing necessary host updates.

### Execution Flow
```text
Props / State / Context
          ↓
       Component
          ↓
      React Elements
          ↓
   Fiber Reconciliation
          ↓
      Render Phase
          ↓
      Commit Phase
          ↓
       Host DOM
          ↓
    Browser Rendering
```

### Component Tree
```text
<App>
 ├── <Shell>
 │    ├── <Navigation>
 │    └── <Content>
 └── <Footer>
```

### Fiber Diagram
```text
Fiber Root
   │
   ├── Fiber(App)
   │      ├── Fiber(Header)
   │      └── Fiber(Main)
   │             └── Fiber(Feature)
   │
   └── alternate → work-in-progress tree
```

### Scheduler Timeline
```text
Urgent input ───────► render/commit
                         │
Non-urgent work ───► can be scheduled around higher-priority work
```

### Advantages
- Clear declarative model
- Strong composition
- Supports scalable UI architecture
- Rich profiling and testing ecosystem

### Disadvantages / Trade-offs
- Abstractions can be overused.
- Rendering behavior can become difficult to reason about in very large trees.
- Performance optimizations add complexity and should be justified by measurement.

### Performance Considerations
- Profile before adding memoization.
- Separate network, CPU, render, commit and browser paint costs.
- Use code splitting and virtualization for the appropriate bottleneck.
- Watch memory retention from subscriptions, closures, caches and long-lived providers.

### Accessibility Considerations
- Prefer native HTML semantics.
- Preserve keyboard and screen-reader behavior.
- Provide accessible loading, error and status states.
- Ensure focus is managed when UI boundaries change.

### Security Considerations
- Treat server data and user input as untrusted.
- Avoid unsafe HTML injection.
- Do not expose secrets in Client Components or browser bundles.
- Audit server/client boundaries and authorization independently of UI visibility.

### Best Practices
- Keep components focused and composable.
- Keep render logic pure.
- Keep state close to its owner.
- Use stable keys for dynamic collections.
- Prefer explicit data boundaries.
- Add telemetry at important production failure boundaries.

### Anti-patterns
- Global state for every value
- Effects used for derived values
- Blind `useMemo` / `useCallback`
- Giant context providers
- Index keys for reorderable lists
- Client-side secrets

### Common Mistakes
- Treating Fiber fields as stable public APIs.
- Assuming a render always equals a DOM mutation.
- Ignoring cleanup and cancellation.
- Optimizing without profiling.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce with the smallest possible component tree.  
2. Use React DevTools Components and Profiler panels.  
3. Inspect props/state/context changes.  
4. Record a performance profile.  
5. Check browser Performance and Network panels.  
6. Add targeted logs rather than broad console noise.

### Common Interview Traps
- Confusing render phase and commit phase.
- Saying concurrent rendering means concurrent DOM mutations.
- Treating `useMemo` as a semantic guarantee.
- Assuming Context is automatically a global-state replacement.

7. What metrics would you monitor in production?

- Keep components focused and composable.
- Keep render logic pure.
- Keep state close to its owner.
- Use stable keys for dynamic collections.
- Prefer explicit data boundaries.
- Add telemetry at important production failure boundaries.

### Anti-patterns
- Global state for every value
- Effects used for derived values
- Blind `useMemo` / `useCallback`
- Giant context providers
- Index keys for reorderable lists
- Client-side secrets

### Common Mistakes
- Treating Fiber fields as stable public APIs.
- Assuming a render always equals a DOM mutation.
- Ignoring cleanup and cancellation.
- Optimizing without profiling.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce with the smallest possible component tree.  
2. Use React DevTools Components and Profiler panels.  
3. Inspect props/state/context changes.  
4. Record a performance profile.  
5. Check browser Performance and Network panels.  
6. Add targeted logs rather than broad console noise.

### Common Interview Traps
- Confusing render phase and commit phase.
- Saying concurrent rendering means concurrent DOM mutations.
- Treating `useMemo` as a semantic guarantee.
- Assuming Context is automatically a global-state replacement.

A production application has a regression involving **State management revision**. Explain how you would identify the root cause, profile it, validate a fix and prevent recurrence.

3. What is the memory cost?

5. How would you test the behavior?
6. What would change at 10× application scale?
7. What metrics would you monitor in production?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion
Define ownership, API boundaries, observability, testing, rollout strategy and failure recovery. For shared infrastructure, document the contract and migration plan before making the abstraction universal.

### System Design Discussion
Design the feature as independently deployable or testable where appropriate. Keep server data, client UI state and cross-cutting configuration distinct. Establish clear performance budgets and failure boundaries.

- [ ] No unnecessary global state
- [ ] Performance measured where optimization is claimed
- [ ] Tests cover user-visible behavior

| Components | Composition | Deep inheritance |
| Lists | Stable identity keys | Index for mutable lists |

## Question 346 — Data fetching revision

**Module:** Module 20 – Final Revision  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐ Medium  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Data fetching revision** to a senior frontend interviewer, and how would you apply it safely in a production React 19+ TypeScript application?

### Definition
Data fetching revision should be understood at API, rendering, runtime and production-architecture levels. A senior engineer should be able to explain its trade-offs, measure its impact, debug failures and choose whether the abstraction belongs in the system.

### Overview
Explain the public React API first, then the rendering consequence, then the production trade-offs. Avoid presenting unstable implementation details as guaranteed public behavior.

### Why It Matters
- It affects correctness, responsiveness, maintainability or scalability.
- Senior interviews expect trade-off analysis, not API memorization.
- Enterprise systems require observability, testing, accessibility and safe migration paths.

### React Internal Behavior
Where applicable, React schedules work, builds/reconciles Fiber trees during rendering, then applies host mutations and runs relevant commit-time work. The exact internal implementation is version-dependent.

### Fiber / Scheduler Flow
```text
Update
  ↓
Priority / Scheduling
  ↓
Work-in-progress Fiber
  ↓
Reconciliation
  ↓
Render
  ↓
Commit
  ↓
Host Environment
```

### Code Example 1
```tsx
type Props = { title: string };

export function Feature({ title }: Props) {
  return <section aria-labelledby="feature-title">
    <h2 id="feature-title">{title}</h2>
  </section>;
}
```

### Code Example 2 — Production Pattern
tsx
import { memo } from "react";

type UserRowProps = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  onOpen: (id: string) => void;
};

export const UserRow = memo(function UserRow({
  id,
  name,
  onOpen,
}: UserRowProps) {
  return (
    <li>
      <span>{name}</span>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => onOpen(id)}>
        Open
      </button>
    </li>
  );
});
```

### Production Example
For a large enterprise application, isolate this concern behind a small feature API, instrument important failures, test user-visible behavior, and measure render/network/browser costs before optimizing.

### Expected Output
The component produces the expected accessible UI. When inputs change, React may schedule rendering work and reconcile the resulting tree before committing necessary host updates.

### Execution Flow
```text
Props / State / Context
          ↓
       Component
          ↓
      React Elements
          ↓
   Fiber Reconciliation
          ↓
      Render Phase
          ↓
      Commit Phase
          ↓
       Host DOM
          ↓
    Browser Rendering
```

### Component Tree
```text
<App>
 ├── <Shell>
 │    ├── <Navigation>
 │    └── <Content>
 └── <Footer>
```

### Fiber Diagram
```text
Fiber Root
   │
   ├── Fiber(App)
   │      ├── Fiber(Header)
   │      └── Fiber(Main)
   │             └── Fiber(Feature)
   │
   └── alternate → work-in-progress tree
```

### Scheduler Timeline
```text
Urgent input ───────► render/commit
                         │
Non-urgent work ───► can be scheduled around higher-priority work
```

### Advantages
- Clear declarative model
- Strong composition
- Supports scalable UI architecture
- Rich profiling and testing ecosystem

### Disadvantages / Trade-offs
- Abstractions can be overused.
- Rendering behavior can become difficult to reason about in very large trees.
- Performance optimizations add complexity and should be justified by measurement.

### Performance Considerations
- Profile before adding memoization.
- Separate network, CPU, render, commit and browser paint costs.
- Use code splitting and virtualization for the appropriate bottleneck.
- Watch memory retention from subscriptions, closures, caches and long-lived providers.

### Accessibility Considerations
- Prefer native HTML semantics.
- Preserve keyboard and screen-reader behavior.
- Provide accessible loading, error and status states.
- Ensure focus is managed when UI boundaries change.

### Security Considerations
- Treat server data and user input as untrusted.
- Avoid unsafe HTML injection.
- Do not expose secrets in Client Components or browser bundles.
- Audit server/client boundaries and authorization independently of UI visibility.

### Best Practices
- Keep components focused and composable.
- Keep render logic pure.
- Keep state close to its owner.
- Use stable keys for dynamic collections.
- Prefer explicit data boundaries.
- Add telemetry at important production failure boundaries.

### Anti-patterns
- Global state for every value
- Effects used for derived values
- Blind `useMemo` / `useCallback`
- Giant context providers
- Index keys for reorderable lists
- Client-side secrets

### Common Mistakes
- Treating Fiber fields as stable public APIs.
- Assuming a render always equals a DOM mutation.
- Ignoring cleanup and cancellation.
- Optimizing without profiling.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce with the smallest possible component tree.  
2. Use React DevTools Components and Profiler panels.  
3. Inspect props/state/context changes.  
4. Record a performance profile.  
5. Check browser Performance and Network panels.  
6. Add targeted logs rather than broad console noise.

### Common Interview Traps
- Confusing render phase and commit phase.
- Saying concurrent rendering means concurrent DOM mutations.
- Treating `useMemo` as a semantic guarantee.
- Assuming Context is automatically a global-state replacement.

- Prefer native HTML semantics.
- Preserve keyboard and screen-reader behavior.
- Provide accessible loading, error and status states.
- Ensure focus is managed when UI boundaries change.

### Security Considerations
- Treat server data and user input as untrusted.
- Avoid unsafe HTML injection.
- Do not expose secrets in Client Components or browser bundles.
- Audit server/client boundaries and authorization independently of UI visibility.

### Best Practices
- Keep components focused and composable.
- Keep render logic pure.
- Keep state close to its owner.
- Use stable keys for dynamic collections.
- Prefer explicit data boundaries.
- Add telemetry at important production failure boundaries.

### Anti-patterns
- Global state for every value
- Effects used for derived values
- Blind `useMemo` / `useCallback`
- Giant context providers
- Index keys for reorderable lists
- Client-side secrets

### Common Mistakes
- Treating Fiber fields as stable public APIs.
- Assuming a render always equals a DOM mutation.
- Ignoring cleanup and cancellation.
- Optimizing without profiling.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce with the smallest possible component tree.  
2. Use React DevTools Components and Profiler panels.  
3. Inspect props/state/context changes.  
4. Record a performance profile.  
5. Check browser Performance and Network panels.  
6. Add targeted logs rather than broad console noise.

### Common Interview Traps
- Confusing render phase and commit phase.
- Saying concurrent rendering means concurrent DOM mutations.
- Treating `useMemo` as a semantic guarantee.
- Assuming Context is automatically a global-state replacement.

### Scenario-Based Question
A production application has a regression involving **Performance revision**. Explain how you would identify the root cause, profile it, validate a fix and prevent recurrence.

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the alternative and why did you reject it?
2. What happens during render versus commit?
3. What is the memory cost?
4. How would React DevTools expose the problem?
5. How would you test the behavior?
6. What would change at 10× application scale?
7. What metrics would you monitor in production?

### Enterprise Architecture Discussion
Define ownership, API boundaries, observability, testing, rollout strategy and failure recovery. For shared infrastructure, document the contract and migration plan before making the abstraction universal.

### System Design Discussion
Design the feature as independently deployable or testable where appropriate. Keep server data, client UI state and cross-cutting configuration distinct. Establish clear performance budgets and failure boundaries.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] Correct React API usage
- [ ] Render logic is pure
- [ ] Cleanup exists for subscriptions/resources
- [ ] Accessibility reviewed
- [ ] Error/loading states handled
- [ ] No unnecessary global state
- [ ] Performance measured where optimization is claimed
- [ ] Tests cover user-visible behavior

### Comparison Table
| Area | Preferred | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| State | Local ownership first | Global by default |
| Performance | Measure → optimize | Blind memoization |
| Async | Cancellation/recovery | Unbounded requests |
| Components | Composition | Deep inheritance |
| Lists | Stable identity keys | Index for mutable lists |

## Question 349 — Testing and accessibility revision

**Module:** Module 20 – Final Revision  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Staff / Principal  
**Experience Level:** 12+ Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
How would you explain **Testing and accessibility revision** to a senior frontend interviewer, and how would you apply it safely in a production React 19+ TypeScript application?

### Definition
Advanced React testing should prioritize user-visible behavior and integration boundaries. Use Testing Library for component behavior, MSW for network boundaries and Playwright/Cypress for critical end-to-end flows.

### Overview
Explain the public React API first, then the rendering consequence, then the production trade-offs. Avoid presenting unstable implementation details as guaranteed public behavior.

### Why It Matters
- It affects correctness, responsiveness, maintainability or scalability.
- Senior interviews expect trade-off analysis, not API memorization.
- Enterprise systems require observability, testing, accessibility and safe migration paths.

### React Internal Behavior
Where applicable, React schedules work, builds/reconciles Fiber trees during rendering, then applies host mutations and runs relevant commit-time work. The exact internal implementation is version-dependent.

### Fiber / Scheduler Flow
```text
Update
  ↓
Priority / Scheduling
  ↓
Work-in-progress Fiber
  ↓
Reconciliation
  ↓
Render
  ↓
Commit
  ↓
Host Environment
```

### Code Example 1
```tsx
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event";
import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";

function SaveButton() {
  return <button type="button">Save</button>;
}

describe("SaveButton", () => {
  it("is keyboard accessible", async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    render(<SaveButton />);
    await user.tab();
    expect(screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" })).toHaveFocus();
  });
});
```

### Code Example 2 — Production Pattern
tsx
import { memo } from "react";

type UserRowProps = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  onOpen: (id: string) => void;
};

export const UserRow = memo(function UserRow({
  id,
  name,
  onOpen,
}: UserRowProps) {
  return (
    <li>
      <span>{name}</span>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => onOpen(id)}>
        Open
      </button>
    </li>
  );
});
```

### Production Example
For a large enterprise application, isolate this concern behind a small feature API, instrument important failures, test user-visible behavior, and measure render/network/browser costs before optimizing.

### Expected Output
The component produces the expected accessible UI. When inputs change, React may schedule rendering work and reconcile the resulting tree before committing necessary host updates.

### Execution Flow
```text
Props / State / Context
          ↓
       Component
          ↓
      React Elements
          ↓
   Fiber Reconciliation
          ↓
      Render Phase
          ↓
      Commit Phase
          ↓
       Host DOM
          ↓
    Browser Rendering
```

### Component Tree
```text
<App>
 ├── <Shell>
 │    ├── <Navigation>
 │    └── <Content>
 └── <Footer>
```

### Fiber Diagram
```text
Fiber Root
   │
   ├── Fiber(App)
   │      ├── Fiber(Header)
   │      └── Fiber(Main)
   │             └── Fiber(Feature)
   │
   └── alternate → work-in-progress tree
```

### Scheduler Timeline
```text
Urgent input ───────► render/commit
                         │
Non-urgent work ───► can be scheduled around higher-priority work
```

### Advantages
- Clear declarative model
- Strong composition
- Supports scalable UI architecture
- Rich profiling and testing ecosystem

### Disadvantages / Trade-offs
- Abstractions can be overused.
- Rendering behavior can become difficult to reason about in very large trees.
- Performance optimizations add complexity and should be justified by measurement.

### Performance Considerations

- Separate network, CPU, render, commit and browser paint costs.
- Use code splitting and virtualization for the appropriate bottleneck.
- Watch memory retention from subscriptions, closures, caches and long-lived providers.

- Client-side secrets

- Ignoring cleanup and cancellation.
- Optimizing without profiling.

- Treating `useMemo` as a semantic guarantee.

# PART 9 – ADVANCED REACT FINAL CHEAT SHEETS

## Fiber / Rendering
```text
Update
 ↓
Schedule
 ↓
Work-in-progress Fiber
 ↓
Render / Reconcile
 ↓
Commit
 ↓
DOM / Host
 ↓
Browser Paint
```

## Concurrency
- Urgent updates should remain responsive.
- Transitions identify non-urgent rendering work.
- Concurrent rendering is interruptible work; it does not mean two independent DOMs are active.
- External stores require concurrency-safe subscription patterns.

## React 19
- Actions
- `useActionState`
- `useOptimistic`
- `useFormStatus`
- Metadata support
- Resource loading APIs
- React Compiler direction
- Server Actions / framework-supported server mutations

## Server Components
```text
Server Component
      ↓
Server Render / RSC Payload
      ↓
Client Component Boundary
      ↓
Hydration / Interactivity
```

## Performance Audit
- [ ] React Profiler trace captured
- [ ] Network waterfall inspected
- [ ] Bundle analyzed
- [ ] Expensive renders identified
- [ ] Context updates checked
- [ ] Memory retention checked
- [ ] Accessibility verified
- [ ] Before/after measurement recorded

## Enterprise Architecture Checklist
- [ ] Feature boundaries
- [ ] API layer
- [ ] Error layer
- [ ] Logging/monitoring
- [ ] Feature flags
- [ ] Design system
- [ ] i18n
- [ ] Testing pyramid
- [ ] CI/CD
- [ ] ADRs

## Senior / Staff / Principal Interview Checklist
- [ ] Fiber and reconciliation
- [ ] Render vs commit
- [ ] Scheduling and concurrency
- [ ] Suspense
- [ ] Server Components
- [ ] React 19 APIs
- [ ] State architecture
- [ ] Data fetching
- [ ] Performance budgets
- [ ] Accessibility governance

- [ ] Enterprise architecture
